summary: The note covers the lion as a cultural symbol across several domains. It explains the origin of Singapore's name from the Malay words singa and pora, the lion's role in Chinese art and the lion dance, its use in heraldry, and its appearances in literature, film and cartoons.
one_line: A survey of the lion's cultural significance in Singapore's naming, Chinese art and dance, heraldry, and modern literature and film.
key_facts: Singapore's name derives from the Malay words singa (lion) and pora (city/fortress).

According to the Malay Annals, fourteenth-century Sumatran Malay prince Sang Nila Utama named Singapore after spotting an auspicious beast that appeared to be a lion on the shore after a thunderstorm.
The lion is a common motif in Chinese art and was first used in art during the late Spring and Autumn period (fifth or sixth century BC).
Lions became more popular during the Han Dynasty (206 BC – AD 220), when imperial guardian lions started to be placed in front of imperial palaces for protection.
Because lions have never been native to China, early depictions of lions in Chinese art were somewhat unrealistic.
After the introduction of Buddhist art to China in the Tang Dynasty after the sixth century AD, lions were usually depicted wingless with shorter, thicker bodies and curly manes.
The lion dance is a traditional Chinese dance in which performers in lion costumes mimic a lion's movements, often with musical accompaniment from cymbals, drums and gongs.
Lion dances are performed at Chinese New Year, the August Moon Festival and other celebratory occasions for good luck.
Lions are frequently depicted on coats of arms, either as a device on shields or as supporters, but the lioness is used much less frequently.
The formal language of heraldry, called blazon, employs French terms to describe images precisely, specifying whether lions are 'rampant' (rearing) or 'passant' (crouching).
The messianic Aslan appears in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe and following books of The Chronicles of Narnia series written by C. S. Lewis.
The comedic Cowardly Lion appears as a character in L. Frank Baum's The Wonderful Wizard of Oz.
Leo has been the mascot for Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM) studios since the 1920s.
The Kenyan lioness Elsa appeared in the 1960s movie Born Free, which is based on the factual book of the same title.

The lion's role as king of the beasts has been used in cartoons such as the 1994 Disney animated feature film The Lion King, the 2005 DreamWorks animated character Alex in Madagascar, and the 2006 Disney animated character Samson in The Wild.
